questions.question_text:
A researcher investigates how a child's age affects their height.
Which option correctly identifies the independent and dependent variables?

options.text: Independent variable: age. Dependent variable: height.
Independent variable: height. Dependent variable: age.
options.why: Reverses the roles: the investigation considers age as a possible influence on height.

options.text: Both age and height are independent variables.
options.why: Treats the outcome, height, as another independent variable.

options.text: Independent variable: the child. Dependent variable: height.
options.why: Names the individual being studied instead of the independent variable, age.

questions.solution_text:
Age is investigated as a possible influence on height.
Independent variable: **age**.
Dependent variable: **height**.

questions.question_text:
A car dealership investigates how a car's engine size affects its fuel efficiency, measured in kilometres per litre.
Which option correctly identifies the independent and dependent variables?

options.text: Independent variable: engine size. Dependent variable: fuel efficiency.
Independent variable: fuel efficiency. Dependent variable: engine size.
options.why: Reverses the roles: engine size is investigated as a possible influence on fuel efficiency.

options.text: Independent variable: the dealership. Dependent variable: fuel efficiency.
options.why: Names the place conducting the investigation instead of the independent variable.

options.text: Independent variable: engine size. Dependent variable: the car.
options.why: Names the individual being studied instead of the measured outcome, fuel efficiency.

questions.solution_text:
Engine size is investigated as a possible influence on fuel efficiency.
Independent variable: **engine size**.
Dependent variable: **fuel efficiency**.

questions.question_text:
Countries that eat more chocolate per person tend to have more Nobel Prize winners per person.
Does this association prove that eating more chocolate causes more Nobel Prizes to be won?

options.text: No — the association alone does not prove a causal link.
Yes — the strong correlation proves chocolate causes higher intelligence.
options.why: Treats a strong correlation as proof of causation, which it never is on its own.

options.text: No — because the two variables are not bivariate data.
options.why: Misapplies the univariate/bivariate classification to a question about causation instead.

options.text: Yes — chocolate must be the cause because it was recorded first in the data.
options.why: Assumes the order variables are listed or recorded in determines which one is the cause.

questions.solution_text:
The two national measures are associated, but this does not show that one causes the other.
National wealth is a possible third factor: it could affect both chocolate purchases and investment in research.
No — the association alone does not prove a causal link.

questions.question_text:
In coastal towns, the number of surf lifesaving club members and the number of sunscreen bottles sold both increase in summer.
Can you conclude from this association that joining a surf club causes people to buy more sunscreen?

options.text: No — the association alone does not prove causation; summer weather could affect both variables.
Yes — both increase at the same time, so club membership must cause sunscreen purchases.
options.why: Treats two variables rising together as proof that one causes the other.

options.text: No — the association proves that sunscreen purchases cause people to join surf clubs instead.
options.why: Treats the same association as proof of the reverse causal direction.

options.text: Yes — listing club membership first makes it the cause.
options.why: Assumes the order in which variables are listed establishes causation.

questions.solution_text:
Both variables rise in summer, but that association alone does not show that joining a surf club causes sunscreen purchases.
Warmer weather could bring more people to the beach, increasing both club membership and sunscreen sales.
No — the association alone does not establish a causal link.

questions.question_text:
A teacher investigates how hours spent watching television affect students' history exam marks.
Which option correctly identifies the independent and dependent variables?

options.text: Independent variable: hours spent watching television. Dependent variable: history exam mark.
Independent variable: history exam mark. Dependent variable: hours spent watching television.
options.why: Reverses the roles: viewing time is investigated as a possible influence on exam marks.

options.text: Both variables are dependent variables because neither proves causation.
options.why: Confuses identifying variable roles with proving a causal relationship.

options.text: Independent variable: the student. Dependent variable: history exam mark.
options.why: Names the individual being studied instead of the independent variable, viewing time.

questions.solution_text:
Television viewing time is investigated as a possible influence on the exam mark.
Independent variable: **hours spent watching television**.
Dependent variable: **history exam mark**.
